title: The DOM and Browser Events
description: Understand the browser's live document tree, select and update elements, handle events, and build a data-driven DOM to-do list.
learningOutcomes: Explain how the browser turns HTML into a live DOM tree.
Select elements safely with querySelector and querySelectorAll.
Create, update and remove DOM nodes through browser APIs.
Choose textContent instead of unsafe HTML insertion for user-controlled text.
Explain event target/currentTarget, bubbling and preventDefault.
Build a small to-do list by updating an array and rendering the current data.

blocks.text: The DOM is the browser's live document model

The HTML source describes a document; the Document Object Model (DOM) is the structured tree the browser creates from that source. JavaScript can inspect or change that tree while the page is open. The DOM is neither a screenshot nor a frozen copy of the original HTML string: nodes can be added, removed, and updated after the browser finishes parsing.
Select nodes and handle missing matches

document.querySelector(selector) returns the first matching element or null. document.querySelectorAll(selector) returns a static NodeList of all current matches. A static NodeList does not automatically include elements inserted after the query. Because a selector can match nothing, check a querySelector result before calling an element method on it.

blocks.text: Create and update nodes with focused APIs

Use createElement to create a node, classList to manage classes, setAttribute for attributes, textContent for plain text, append to insert nodes, and remove to detach one. These APIs keep content and structure separate. For user-provided strings, textContent is safer than interpreting that data as HTML.

blocks.title: Do not inject user input into innerHTML
blocks.text: innerHTML parses a string as markup. Concatenating untrusted input into it can enable cross-site scripting (XSS). Prefer createElement plus textContent for ordinary user text; only parse trusted or properly sanitized HTML when there is a clear reason.

blocks.text: Events connect user actions to code

addEventListener registers a callback that the browser runs when an element receives an event such as click, input, or submit. event.target identifies where the event originated; event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently running. Many events bubble to ancestors, making event delegation possible, but not every event bubbles.

blocks.prompt: What does querySelector return when there is no matching element?

options.feedback: querySelector returns null when no element matches.
querySelector returns one element or null; it does not return an array.
querySelectorAll returns a NodeList; querySelector returns one element or null.
The documented no-match result is null.

blocks.explanation: Check for null before calling methods on a queried element.

blocks.prompt: Assigning a user-provided string to textContent parses any HTML tags in that string into DOM elements.

options.feedback: textContent treats the input as text and does not parse tags into elements.
HTML parsing is performed by APIs such as innerHTML; textContent supplies text.

blocks.explanation: Use text APIs for ordinary user-controlled content to reduce markup injection risk.

blocks.prompt: Which statements about browser events are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: event.target is where the event originated
options.feedback: The target points to the original event source.

options.text: event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running
options.feedback: currentTarget refers to the element on which the active listener is registered.

options.text: Every event bubbles through all ancestors
options.feedback: Bubbling behavior depends on the event type.

options.text: preventDefault automatically validates and stores the form
options.feedback: It cancels a default action; validation and persistence need separate logic.

blocks.title: Build a data-driven DOM to-do list
blocks.context: Use an array as the source of truth and browser DOM APIs to display tasks. The platform stores your draft; JavaScript execution is available in the separate sandbox only for synchronous examples, not for the DOM scaffold in this exercise.
instructions: Select the form, text input, and list container.
Keep tasks in an array of objects with id, title, and completed fields.
Create renderTasks() that clears the list and creates one li per task.
On form submit, prevent the default action, trim the input, and ignore a blank title.
Update the tasks array before calling renderTasks().
Use textContent for task titles and explain why innerHTML is unsafe for arbitrary user text.
Support removing a task with a button and event delegation, or document the removal design.
Test empty input, multiple tasks, and calling renderTasks more than once.
requirements: The array is the source of truth; the DOM is derived from it.
The form submit event is handled on the form itself.
Empty or whitespace-only titles are ignored.
User-provided titles are rendered as text rather than HTML.
Repeated rendering does not duplicate visible list items.
The learner can explain null selectors, event targets, and preventDefault.
hints: Update the array first, then call renderTasks().
Clear or reconcile previous child nodes before rendering again.
Use createElement and textContent for user-supplied title strings.
successCriteria: A non-empty submit creates one item in the model and one visible list item.
A blank submit creates no task.
Repeated renderTasks calls do not duplicate items.
The solution does not concatenate arbitrary user text into HTML.
You can explain how state changes lead to rendered output.

items: The DOM is the browser's live document tree; querySelector returns an element or null.
Use createElement, textContent, classList, setAttribute, append, and remove for deliberate DOM updates.
Use addEventListener for browser interactions and distinguish target, currentTarget, bubbling, and default actions.
Handle submit on the form and call preventDefault only when replacing normal submission behavior.
For a small to-do app, keep an array as source of truth and render the visible list from it.
